How to calculate income tax in Estonia (2026)

Estonia taxes pay at a flat 22% after a tax-free allowance of €700 a month. Employees also pay 1.6% unemployment insurance and, by default, 2% into the second pension pillar. On €36,000 a year an employee pays about €5,787 in income tax and keeps about €28,917 (80.3%). With no second-pillar contribution, they keep about €29,479 (81.9%).

What the law says

The figures below are the 2026 rates as the calculator models them, in euros. Estonia has one national income tax rate, so there is no municipality to choose, though local governments receive part of the revenue. The calculator models an employee on one salary for a full year.

Flat income tax and the tax-free allowance

Income is taxed at a flat 22%. Each month you can claim a tax-free allowance of €700 (€8,400 a year), and the calculator also has a setting for the higher €776 allowance. Taxable income is pay minus unemployment insurance, pension pillar II contributions and the allowance.

Employee contributions

Employees pay unemployment insurance of 1.6% of pay. Contributions to the second pension pillar are 2% by default, and the calculator lets you choose 0%, 2%, 4% or 6%. Both are deducted before income tax is worked out, so they lower your taxable income.

What the employer pays on top

The employer pays social tax of 33% on top of your gross salary, so it does not reduce your take-home pay. It is part of the cost of hiring you, and it funds the state pension and health insurance. The calculator shows only what you pay.

Sources

  • Estonian Tax and Customs Board (EMTA), income tax, allowance, employer social tax
  • Pensionikeskus, second and third pension pillars
  • Estonian Police and Border Guard Board, residence permits and registration

Worked examples

How to calculate Estonian income tax on a €36,000 salary

This is an employee earning €36,000 with the default 2% pillar II contribution. Unemployment insurance takes €576 and pillar II takes €720. The €8,400 allowance is then deducted, leaving taxable income of €26,304. At 22% the income tax is €5,787. You keep about €28,917, or 80.3% of gross.

  1. Gross paya year, before tax€36,000
  2. Unemployment insurance (1.6%)contribution, taken from pay−€576
  3. Pension pillar II (2%)contribution, taken from pay−€720
  4. Tax-free allowance (700 a month)lowers the taxable income€8,400
  5. Income tax (22%)tax, taken from pay−€5,787
  6. Take-home pay80.3% of gross, €2,410 a month€28,917

Your marginal rate is 24.8%: the 22% tax, the 1.6% unemployment insurance and the 2% pillar II contribution, less the tax each of those contributions saves.

Estonian take-home pay on €36,000 without the second pension pillar

This is the same employee who chooses 0% for pillar II. Without the €720 contribution, taxable income is €27,024, and income tax is €5,945, which is about €158 more. Unemployment insurance of €576 still applies. You keep about €29,479, or 81.9% of gross, about €562 more than with pillar II.

  1. Gross paya year, before tax€36,000
  2. Unemployment insurance (1.6%)contribution, taken from pay−€576
  3. Tax-free allowance (700 a month)lowers the taxable income€8,400
  4. Income tax (22%)tax, taken from pay−€5,945
  5. Take-home pay81.9% of gross, €2,457 a month€29,479

The extra take-home pay is not free. Pillar II money goes into a pension account in your own name, so you are choosing between cash now and retirement savings. Confirm what you can choose with the Pensionikeskus.

How to pay less tax, legally

These are mainstream, legal ways to manage Estonian tax. Which ones apply depends on your status.

Decide on the second pension pillar

Suits: anyone who can choose. The pillar II contribution lowers your taxable income, so about 22% of it comes back as lower tax, and it builds a pension in your own name.

Caveat: whether you can join, change or stop depends on your age and history, so check your options at the Pensionikeskus.

Use the third pension pillar

Suits: residents who want to save more for retirement. Voluntary contributions to a third-pillar pension can reduce taxable income within a limit set by law.

Caveat: the limit and conditions change, and the money is locked until retirement age. Look up the current rule with EMTA.

Claim the allowance at one employer only

Suits: anyone with more than one job. The €700 monthly allowance can be applied by one payer at a time, so tell your main employer to use it.

Caveat: if two payers apply it, you may owe tax when you file the annual return.

What the calculator does not model

  • Employment income only. It models one salary for a full year. Business income, dividends and a part year are not included.
  • Flat allowance. The calculator applies €700 a month, or €776 if you tick the box, and nothing else that depends on your income.
  • No other deductions. Housing loan interest, training costs and similar deductions are not modelled.
  • No employer costs. The 33% social tax is not shown in your take-home pay.
  • Rates change. Estonian rates and allowances have been revised in recent years, so confirm the current figures with EMTA.
  • No bonuses, equity or tax treaties. Share options and foreign tax credits are not modelled.

General information, not tax advice. The figures follow the rules as published for the year shown. Check the ones that matter to you with the tax authority or an adviser before you sign a contract.

Frequently asked questions

How much tax do I pay on €36,000 in Estonia?

An employee pays about €5,787 in income tax, plus €576 unemployment insurance and €720 into pillar II, and keeps about €28,917. Try your own figure in the Global Income Tax Calculator.

Is the €700 tax-free allowance really monthly?

Yes. It applies each month, which is €8,400 a year in the calculator. You claim it through one payer at a time. If you have two jobs, the allowance should go to your main one, and the second employer withholds without it. Any difference is settled in your annual tax return.

Do I have to pay into the second pension pillar?

It is a choice for many people, which is why Estonia is unusual. The calculator uses 2% by default and lets you set 0%, 2%, 4% or 6%. A contribution lowers your taxable income and builds a pension in your name. Check your own options with the Pensionikeskus.

Does the pension contribution reduce my income tax?

Yes. Unemployment insurance and pillar II contributions are deducted before the 22% applies. In the example the €720 contribution lowers tax by about €158, so the real cost to you is about €562.

Who pays the 33% social tax?

Your employer pays it on top of your gross salary. It is not deducted from your pay and the calculator does not include it in your take-home figure, but it is part of what you cost to hire.
